subtopic: TREATMENT OF SURPLUS EMPLOYEES- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
subtopic: TREATMENT OF SURPLUS EMPLOYEES- REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a motion under Standing Order 43, which provides that in a case of urgent and pressing necessity, previously explained by the mover, a motion be made by unanimous consent of the House without notice having been given under Standing Order 42. I shall state briefly the reason for this motion which I think is of urgent and pressing necessity.
On December 16 last the Public Service Commission recommended to all deputy ministers that in its opinion a review procedure should be established with respect to surplus employees being given notices of dismissal. It appears that this recommendation has not yet been acted on by the Department of Fisheries and Forestry. Hence a good deal of concern is felt by the scientists in particular who are being laid off from their employment in that department. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask leave of the House, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orlikow), to move as follows:
That this House recommends to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry that a review procedure for surplus employees be established within his department, as recommended by the Public Service Corn-21701-36
mission on December 16, 1969, and that the dismissal of surplus employees by this department be suspended until the opportunity for review in all cases has been provided.
I may say that we would be quite prepared to forgo any debate on this motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. A. Olson (Minister of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: AGRICULTURAL PRODUCTS CO-OPERATIVE MARKETING ACT AMENDMENT OF DEFINITION OF "AGRICULTURAL PRODUCT"
speechtext:
that Bill C-183, to amend the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as hon. members will be aware, this bill makes a very small amendment to the Agricultural Products Cooperative Marketing Act but, in my opinion, it is a very important amendment for the wheat growers of eastern Canada, and particularly Ontario. I should advise Your Honour that we have reached an agreement through the usual channels to adjourn this debate at one o'clock and, if we finish the second reading stage before one o'clock, to ask the unanimous consent of the House to have the bill considered in committee of the whole instead of referring it to the standing committee, in order that we may deal with this small but important amendment.
This Act became law in 1939. The general objective of the act is to promote the orderly marketing of agricultural products. Under the legislation a group of producers wishing to market products collectively may enter into an agreement with the Minister of Agriculture. These agreements provide for a guarantee of bank loans covering initial payments, processing, carrying and selling costs.
Under the Act the initial payment to producers must not exceeed 80 per cent of the average price paid to producers according to grade and quality over the three year period preceding the year of production. It also provides that equal returns must be made to primary producers for agricultural products of like grade and quality. Further, it provides that final returns must be made to primary producers of the proceeds of the sale of the product after deducting processing, carrying and selling costs.
Many producer groups in different provinces have used or considered using this legis-
(Mr. Mcllraith.]
lation from time to time and, since 1939 when the Act came into force, a variety of agricultural products have been marketed under the act. Chief among these have been forage crop seeds, potatoes, ranch-bred fox pelts, fresh apples and apples for processing, maple syrup, tobacco, and beans. At the present time there are agreements under the provisions of the Act with respect to the marketing of processed apples in Quebec and beans in Ontario.
The purpose of this amendment is to include wheat, other than that grown in the designated area under the Canadian Wheat Board Act. Currently wheat is excluded, because at the time this act became law all wheat was under the Canadian Wheat Board Act which provided, as hon. members know, for initial payments, pooling and things of that nature. Since World War II, Ontario has not been part of the designated area under the Canadian Wheat Board Act and, therefore, is excluded from the initial payments, pooling provisions and measures of that sort embodied in the Act. Ontario wheat producers have been giving serious consideration to marketing their wheat on a pool basis, with initial payments being paid to producers on delivery. As a result, the Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board has requested this type of amendment. With this amendment the Ontario producers would have available to them the same legislation that is available to other agricultural producers.
As hon. members well know, Mr. Speaker, and as I said at the outset, this amendment is simply to change the definition of agricultural product to mean any kind of grain, other than wheat, that is grown in an area that is defined as a designated area by the Canadian Wheat Board Act. There are no other amendments here.
We believe that we should respond to the request of the Ontario Wheat Producer's Marketing Board so that if they decide to pool the wheat grown in any year in Ontario they could take advantage of the guarantees of credit that are available by the Department of Agriculture under this Act. If the producers received these payments, they could perhaps have larger volumes of credit available to them and perhaps even at a more favourable rate of interest.
If the House concludes second reading before one o'clock, I will be asking for consent to go into Committee of the Whole so that we can dispose of this small amendment to the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the minister for the courtesy he has shown the House by the fullness of his explanation regarding this amendment to the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act. The minister is correct in his assumption that this seems to be a minor amendment to an Act which is already part of the law of Canada. However, it is of particular significance to the producers of wheat in eastern Canada, particularly in the province that I have the honour to represent.
I am very pleased by the indication of the minister that he wishes this particular measure to go before the Committee of the Whole. Since it is of particular significance to one part of Canada, I think we can make much better progress that way than by referring it to the standing committee for consideration. In committee the Ontario members in particular will be asking many questions for clarification of what the government proposes, its powers and plans for this particular commodity.
I wish to give some background of the workings of the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board at the present time, and some of the problems they have been encountering. It is my understanding they have been negotiatmg with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to see whether a change in the statute might make it possible for them to act in a manner which would be of more benefit to the farmers they represent. I would like to point out that I am very much indebted to my colleague, the hon. member for Huron (Mr. McKinley) for many of the facts I wish to present today. With his very close association with the Wheat Board over the years, he has become very knowledgeable in this particular field. He has provided the real basic background for my remarks today.
The wheat growers in Ontario belong to a marketing board known as the Ontario Wheat Producers' Marketing Board. This board was formed under provincial legislation. It has been the aim and object of this particular board, in representing the farmers to produce wheat in Ontario, to sell this commodity at the very best possible price and to negotiate each year a floor price below which no grower is forced to sell. A request was made after World War II, that this particular commodity be removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board because this type of wheat is not the same as that which is normally grown in the west. It has a different growing period, and is not the same in pro-

Agricultural Products Co-op Marketing Act tein content or composition. It is used for blending and many other purposes for which western wheat is not normally used.
As is its custom, the board last year again negotiated a floor price for the wheat offered for sale by the Ontario farmers. In order to make the floor price stable, the board agreed to buy any wheat for which a ready market could not be found at the established price. During the period July 1, 1968 to June 30, 1969, which is the end of their year, the board carried forward 374,000 bushels of the 1966 wheat crop which had not been sold. They also carried forward 3,536,000 bushels of the
1967	wheat crop. They purchased 3,700,000 bushels of the 1968 wheat crop, making a total of 7,610,000 bushels from these three crops. I am happy to announce that by the end of September last, the board had sold the 1966 crop carry-over and a rebate of 6.11 cents was issued to 22,000 producers who had contributed to the 1966 crop.
There is a deduction from the selling price of the current crop which the Board uses to finance its operations and to cover the necessary expenditures when buying the surplus wheat. By the end of November last, the board had sold the 1967 crop carryover and had accrued a loss which was taken out of the reserve fund. Two major contracts accounted for the bulk of sales. Only minor quantities moved in the domestic feed market.

As I say, I feel we have in some ways given away the authority both of the House and of the individual to the Governor in Council as a result of certain measures passed in the last few years.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this stage in the progress of Bill C-12, which would establish the International Development Research Centre of Canada, having had a profitable session in committee, it is a privilege for me to make some remarks with regard to this forward looking and very essential legislation which I think can open, if it is developed and used properly, a new era for Canada in its international role.
I was a bit disturbed yesterday to read that the OECD, in their recent report, published the fact that Canada's position as it relates to the development assistance committee of the OECD was the last of 17 nations who make up that committee. These figures of course were not for 1969. They were for the year 1968 and therefore they do not represent the latest statistics concerning what Canada has been able to do in development assistance in the world. But nevertheless they are significant, in that, of the net flow of Canadian official and private resources to developing countries in 1968, was, the lowest in terms of percentage of national income of all the member countries of that committee.
I will not go into the various supplementary aspects of that because I do not want to take up the time of the House, but it points up the fact that we really are not yet doing what we should be doing so far as international development is concerned. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is my intention in commenting on this bill today to deal with the over-all aspects of the responsibility of Canada to the world so far as the less developed nations are concerned.
It seems to me that Canada, as a nation, has had great difficulty in searching for and finding a national image, at least in the conventional sense of national identity and sovereignty. In some respects this search for a national image has been a hopeless search, and there are several reasons why this has been true. First, the enormous size of the country and its own regional diversities have prevented a homogeneous national culture from developing. Second the English and the French and the multi-ethnic groups have tended to emphasize their differences rather than developing a unified front. In times of emergency, such as World War II and World War I, there has been an exception to this. I think it is correct to say that we really have not been able to acquire a sense of national identity or present a uniform national front in this nation as some other nations have.
3908	COMMONS DEBATES	February 20, 1970
International Development Research Centre
[DOT] (2:10 p.m.)
Third, and I think this is of very real importance to us, the sense of nationalism has become stronger in the world and the influence of our neighbour, the world's strongest, most affluent and dynamic nation, has infiltrated every aspect of Canadian life and thinking. As a result, we have failed to develop a sense of national autonomy and purpose. Perhaps we, ourselves, are least able to see this. Having travelled around the world a good bit, I have seen how others look at us. Their picture of Canada is clearer than our own, and clearer, particularly, than the image of those Canadians who examine themselves. Paradoxically, it is not so difficult for outsiders to examine our raison d'etre and our particular characteristics or identity. Yet in this rather unorthodox situation a new strength was developing even before we were aware of it.
Hand in hand with this has come a new world concept of togetherness as communications and improved travel have brought the peoples of the world closer together. Barbara Ward has described the world as a global village. With this, nationalism, as it has been understood for centuries and up to Hitler's day, has become far too costly a luxury for the modern world. The only hope for mankind is to define new mechanisms less politically divisive in nature. I think that Canada, as a result of its experience in dealing with its own problems and the experience of people within it in living harmoniously together, is uniquely equipped to be a model for such a political instrumentality.
We are an ex-colony and, as most ex-colonies would like to be, are better equipped than the British, better equipped than the French and better equipped even than the United States to experiment and create more flexible forms of government which might bridge the differences between separate communities of peoples of widely divergent backgrounds and outlook. Likewise, it has become apparent that we might be able to lead the way in assisting with these global differences long before others have even comprehended the problems in devising new arrangements and organizations which will enhance the benefits of international integration. In reality, this adds up to Canada having a chance to become the world's first international nation and to move to the front of an emerging global order in the next century, instead of continuing to worry about our own failures to realize the more nationalistic goals of the last century.

I am convinced that the most practical means of accomplishing the goal I have referred to, at the beginning at least, will be in the area of development assistance or international development, if one wishes to call it that. May I clarify that statement? There are at least three aspects of foreign aid which could more properly be termed "international development". On the subject may I say this: first, the idea that international development is a form of charity must be rejected. There are definite reasons for this. So far as Canada is concerned, 60 per cent of all aid funds are spent in Canada; in the United States the figure is almost 90 per cent. Thus "aid" as such is a substantial subsidy to the domestic economy, giving jobs to Canadians and providing other benefits. Home benefits, therefore, automatically eliminate the word "foreign" from development assistance programs. Why do I say that, Mr. Speaker? I say it because the aid is mutual. Likewise, such programs are not "aid" either but represent investments in people and prosperity, and in peace and freedom.
There was a day when international relief could be called charity but such terminology has long outlived the true nature of development assistance because the emphasis has shifted from relief to recovery and to development. International development in its basic concept goes even farther; it becomes a partnership in an international joint venture to relieve human degradation and misery and to expand the world economy. Second, international development relates directly to trade. We cannot sell to an impoverished country simply because such a nation cannot buy or sell. A developing nation is a nation with a developing market and, together, the developing countries form a vast, potential market. They represent the new economic frontier of the future.
Then, too, the flow of capital to the developing areas of the world must be greatly increased. It is estimated that 85 per cent of the developing world's development effort is self-generated. The extra 15 per cent which is needed represents the crucial portion which must come from outside. Successful economic progress for these countries depends on outside capital. Without it they fail, and this has been true of Canada in the past and may be true of Canada at this time. The tragedy of the situation in which the rich nations become richer and the developing nations poorer is that, instead of development and growth, in these latter countries there is a retardation of economic growth and viability.
February 20, 1970	COMMONS
In recent years, the developed nations of the world have been growing richer by about $60 billion per year. The United States alone adds some $50 billion a year to its wealth, which is more than the total gross national product of all African countries put together. The flow of capital aid has in the last seven years increased from $6 billion to about $8 billion, but more than half of this comes back to the developed nations in the form of loan repayments and interest charges. Thus, the flow of capital aid is actually decreasing, because the rich are becoming richer and the poor poorer. It is, therefore, possible for the developed countries to increase their development assistance from their own growth rates without in any way endangering their present living standards and affluence. It is this concept which I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, must be more clearly understood; it is in this area that the International Development Research Centre of Canada can perform tremendous service.
At the past session of the United Nations, Canada moved a resolution which would provide for the total mobiliza'ion of public opinion on the subject of international development. This resolution, which received the assent of the United Nations General Assembly, is indicative of the need for a much greater effort than has been exerted in the past in our understanding of international development. We are not yet keeping up, in the giving of aid, with the expansion of our own economies.
Having said these things, Mr. Speaker, I state without equivocation that this is a good bill. I believe it will move us forward in the right direction and will meet a need in the area of international development to which I have referred. It will enable this country to assume a more effective leadership role in world development. Bill C-12 calls for the establishment of an institution which will be named the International Development Research Centre of Canada. It will be an independent, non-profit organization with an international character. The planned purpose of the centre will be to ini'iate, encourage, support, and undertake research into the problems involved in the development of the economically underdeveloped regions of the world. It will focus its attention particularly on the adaptation and application of scientific and technological knowledge to the needs of the peoples of those regions for social and economic development. It will also endeavour
DEBATES	3909
International Development Research Centre to assist these people to develop their own capabilities to solve the problems of economic underdevelopment which confront them.
[DOT] (2:20 p.ra.)
It is expected that the centre will enlist, as the bill states, the talents of natural and social scientists and technologists, not only from Canada but from all over the world. As expressed in committee and in this debate, these activities will be directed to the identification of specific development problems and the use of multi-disciplinary techniques in devising practical solutions for them. I say, Mr. Speaker, this is the idealistic potential of this organization. Whether the organization moves in to accomplish those objectives will depend entirely upon the men who are given the responsibility, the president and the board, to give direction to the development centre. They can flub the ball and the centre will not make any great contribution, or they can take hold of it and use it as a vehicle to make Canada a real leader in this area of international development.
In spite of the fact our contribution may have gone down in 1968, was not nearly what it should have been in 1969 and it does not appear it will be what we would like it to be in 1970, this bill puts us in front of many other nations because of the vehicle that it will establish, provided that vehicle can be used. As I understand the bill, and as I see its potential, the Development Research Centre could become strictly a vehicle for research for our own academics and for the academics who may share in the operation and work of this research centre. If this is all it accomplishes, it will have gained only a very small portion of its potential. I believe the research conducted at this centre will have to be directed at the practical side of international development.
If some of the things I outlined in these three points are brought about, it will have to become much more than a research centre. It will have to give guidelines and direction to the over-all picture of international development, not only as it relates to the development that comes from this country, but also to the development which is planned by other countries. It is an interesting fact that a number of the middle power nations are paving the way. I believe they will give the greatest support to this research centre. I speak of the Scandinavian countries, Holland, West Germany and some other countries. As a middle power we have a very unique role,
3S10	COMMONS
International Development Research Centre to play to bring about the satisfactory integration that must be brought about in the economic development of the world.
I believe that this bill brings into being an institution that will keep its sights on the over-all perspective and will concentrate on the various areas of research that must have attention. At the same time, it must have as its basic goal the direction of that research and the outcome of that research into the fundamental and basic international development that the world today needs, not just the developed world but also the emerging world. When viable economies are developed in these countries, true international development will make them what we want them to be. I am very pleased to say that we give our support to the principle and over-all objective of this bill.

My remarks on this occasion will relate particularly to the amendments proposed by the standing committee. Several clauses of the bill have been significantly altered. The international responsibilities of the Research Centre have been recognized by omitting ref-21701-37
International Development Research Centre erence to its location from the title. The outmoded term of the 'sixties, "economically underdeveloped" has been revised to read "developing", anticipating the thrust of the 'seventies.
The objects of the Centre have been expanded to allow for the very necessary role of co-ordination of international development research conducted both in Canada and elsewhere. The composition of the Board of Governors of the Research Centre has been altered in such a way as to ensure maximum representation from other countries, especially developing countries, without sacrificing Canadian control over policy and expenditures.
I have no quarrel with these amendments; indeed, I believe they are most valuable and that is why I was pleased to support them. I do, however, Mr. Speaker, wish to express my reservations with respect to clause 10(3). This subclause reads:
One of the governors who is a Canadian citizen other than the Chairman and the Vice-chairman may be a Member of Parliament; he shall not be paid remuneration, but shall be eligible for expenses and shall not, by reason of his being the holder of the office or place in respect of which such expenses are payable, be rendered incapable of being elected, or of sitting or voting as a member of the House of Commons.

It may be progressive; I would not argue that for a moment. But it is an innovation, and it is therefore of some considerable importance that we should be approving an appointment to the board of an agency of government, of a Member of Parliament. I am not certain myself whether in fact this could not have been done in the absence of an amendment. But the amendment has made it clear that if a Member of Parliament is appointed to a board of the Centre, he does not thereby lose his seat in the House of Commons by accepting expenses from the Crown. I understand that those who support this addition to the bill have expressed the belief that a Member of Parliament could serve as a means of liaison between the Centre and Parliament.
I welcome this expression of interest in the working of the Centre and I share this desire to see that Parliament is kept informed of the important work to be carried out by the new institution. However, I do feel the proposal raises some major questions which can neither be ignored nor entirely settled here

International Development Research Centre today. I consider it my responsibility as a member of the government to raise certain fundamental questions and to express a view concerning the nature of the real relationship between Parliament and a government agency created by and, ultimately, answerable to Parliament. This question raises the subject of the responsibility and role of the minister and of the Member of Parliament. It is of such importance that it cannot be resolved by making an insertion to any one clause of a particular bill. If Parliament wants to adopt this practice it should examine its implications in detail and provide legislation and criteria which would be broadly applicable to all the relevant Crown-created institutions.
The role of the Member of Parliament on the Board of .Governors is by no means clear and this uncertainty poses real difficulties for the M.P. himself, the Centre and the Government. One of the standard biases which has served most newspapers pretty well for generations is that of news interest. Mind you, the interpretation of what is news is difficult. The interpretation of what is news interest is debated among newspapermen now just as it was 25 years ago when I first began to report. One could argue, I suggest, that the totality of such information, which is one-sided, might make any decision difficult unless at the same time there is access on the part of the public to the parliamentary process. Unless we as parliamentarians are willing to tolerate radio and television coverage of the chamber and committees, we may discover to our sorrow that although the people may be better informed as to the position the government takes on various issues, a full discussion of any related issue might be disconnected, entirely lost or even suppressed.
There has been a further development in our parliamentary system which lends itself most usefully to coverage by radio and television media. During the past few years greater and greater demands have been made to develop the role of parliamentary committees as centres for more extensive and thoughtful discussion of major issues being considered. Although we may not expect to see either House or committee proceedings covered regularly by the media, there may be issues which present themselves from time to time which I believe can be covered effectively through the use of radio and television.

My resolution reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider ways of preventing oil drilling in west coast Canadian waters where accidental oil leakage could create a major disaster in this busy industrial, recreational and residential area.
Much has been said in the House of Commons about this subject in recent days and weeks, particularly in view of the tragic circumstances off the Atlantic coast involving the sinking of an oil tanker. This event has drawn to our attention even more forcibly the danger that can arise to our coastline as a result of oil drilling programs. This is especially so in areas where there is very considerable tourist and pleasure traffic; where marine life abounds; where we are doing our best to preserve and to protect marine life; where people use the beaches; where there are many marinas and pleasure boats in operation; where recreation is part of the business and life of the community along the shore, and where residences overlook waters or are located at beach areas. The purpose of the resolution is to protect areas such as the Gulf of Georgia and other waters off the west coast, for example the west coast of Vancouver Island, the area of Long Beach and other points that are now being developed for tourist and recreational purposes.
We have been watching the search of the oil companies for oil in the Gulf of Georgia with considerable alarm. Members of this House from the west coast have gone to see the Minister of Energy, Mines and Kesources (Mr. Greene) to urge upon him that licences for drilling in this area do not issue. The Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) has gone so far as to declare in a public address that he believes oil drilling in the Gulf of Georgia should never take place; further, that this area should be a national park to preserve for all time the waters in the Strait of Georgia as a national reserve, an area where oil drilling and oil spillage should be minimized so as to protect the recreational facilities in the vicinity for the benefit of people in the coastal region. It was a tragedy when oil leakages as a result of drilling occurred on the floor of the coast, destroying marine life, birds and wildlife for many miles along the coast.
We have been told that the nature of the wildlife and marine life along the coast has undergone a change; that indeed it may never be restored as a result of this tragic accident. Even more important is it to fear an accident in the Gulf of Georgia, waters that are confined between Vancouver Island and the

I assure the hon. member it is embarrassing and difficult because, as I said, it is precisely this type of attitude by the provinces which causes problems in the fight against pollution. If the hon. member wishes us to act in British Columbia as he suggests, like a bull in a china shop, and have every issue on pollution go to the Supreme Court on constitutional grounds, that may be his idea of what we should do. I suggest we might do precisely the same in the case of Manitoba.
I suggest to him, further, that we will probably do a great deal more to solve the problem of pollution by dealing with the provincial premiers as reasonable men, and I am sure he would agree that Premier Schreyer and Premier Bennett are reasonable men. If he wishes to tackle pollution problems by confrontation with the provinces, I am glad his party is far from power. Let me add that this centralist NDP concept concerning the concentration of power in Ottawa is a traditional attitude of theirs, and is something about which they are not ashamed. They make it a perfectly open part of their platform. But let me point out to them that if they wish to go ahead with that type of approach, they will probably prevent any real solution of many of the problems of water pollution which involve both federal and provincial governments, even in the NDP governed province of Manitoba.
I wish to turn now to the specific question of oil drilling in British Columbia which, as I said, is not so very different from the case in Manitoba at Whitewater Lake. I should like to point out that the motion put forward by

the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Deachman) is precisely the type of motion which the House can go on record as approving. It is a resolution which might help to prevent damage which would be possible if drilling takes place in the Gulf of Georgia and in Manitoba, if the province of Manitoba does not change its mind about drilling there.
It is this careful, cautious approach to preserve the wildlife, to preserve the beauty and to preserve the heritage of Canada which I most heartily endorse. The same is true with respect to the north, if the hon. member for Kootenay West will allow me a few more words on some other area of Canada apart from the west coast. In the north, where again we do not know enough about the possible effects of drilling, we should also have this type of ban.
I should like to go on record as supporting most heartily the proposal of the Canadian Wildlife Federation which calls for a ban on drilling in the Arctic until such time as more is known about the potential damage to the ecology of the area as a result of such drilling. The same is true in British Columbia; we should do precisely the same thing in the Gulf of Georgia. Part of the Gulf of Georgia is in my riding and part is in the riding of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), who happens to be away this afternoon. It is an area of great beauty, a great potential tourist attraction; indeed, it already has a great tourist industry. It is an area which would be threatened very severely if drilling were permitted there.
It is perhaps not commonly known to members representing other parts of Canada that Vancouver Island and the west coast of Canada lie in the same general earthquake belt as Santa Barbara and San Francisco. This belt stretches to Alaska, and members will recall the disastrous earthquake which took place in Alaska not so long ago. What would happen if drilling took place in the Gulf of Georgia, even if precautions were taken, and an earthquake occurred and severed the wells? We would have the same problem as was experienced in Santa Barbara. Oil would seep up along the whole rift along the ocean floor, and there would be no possible way of stopping that seepage because the oil would be seeping, not from the well but from many different cracks in the surface of the ocean floor.
We would be faced with the same situation as in Santa Barbara where it was quite
DEBATES	3929
Oil Drilling in West Coast Waters impossible to properly clean up the oil. Mr. Speaker, at Santa Barbara seals were covered with oil. For a time they stayed alive and continued to swim, but slowly, one by one they died until finally in some areas they were wiped out entirely. The same was true of other wildlife, and indeed the same may be true of salmon and other fish. If it happened in Canada, in the Gulf of Georgia, instead of Canada's most beautiful recreational area, we would have a water desert and a water wasteland. The proposal of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra would prevent that type of disaster occurring. It is for this reason that I endorse it most heartily.
I also endorse most heartily the proposal that the whole area of the Gulf of Georgia become a national park. As hon. members have mentioned, there is no difficulty with the province over jurisdiction because this is a totally federal area. There is no question of adopting the bull in the china shop tactics proposed by the hon. member for Kootenay West in this area, because the Gulf of Georgia is entirely a federal area. Therefore, the proposal that the entire sea bed, and the waters about the sea-bed right up to the high water mark of the Gulf of Georgia, become a national park and an area where we could have, for example, tourist submarines such as the Swiss have in Lake Geneva, where people can go down and see marine life in the water, is an excellent one. Perhaps if technology advances sufficiently every family will have its own little yellow submarine for this purpose.
This is the kind of area we must preserve for the future. We cannot allow this whole area, its present recreational value as well as its potential value, to be jeopardized by oil drilling. If, for example, we were told by geologists that the Gulf of Georgia was the richest and most profitable oil pool in the world, that it rivalled Kuwait or some of the Middle East kingdoms, we might be tempted to weigh the recreational value of the area against its value in oil. But every single piece of evidence we have indicates that it is not that type of situation at all, and that any oil that might be found in the Gulf of Georgia would be of marginal value and would not be great because evidently the geological formation is shallow. Thus, if we decided to drill we would be risking tremendous loss for a very hypothetical gain.
Mr. Speaker, this motion encompasses more than the Gulf of Georgia; it deals with the whole west coast of Canada. The proposal has

Fortunately, the wells turned out to be dry, if you can describe wells beneath the sea as being dry. In any event, there was no oil. They were capped, the capping was evidently satisfactory and thus they will not leak in the future.
Nevertheless, because that whole area is in an earthquake zone and, with the present technology, it is not possible to prevent similar disasters as that which occurred in the Santa Barbara channel from arising, I feel that the motion of the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra would be most applicable in that area as well. Recently we have stocked this area with the sea otter, which was the first reason for white men coming to the coast of British Columbia. My friend, the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Mar-chand), sitting behind me today, may doubt that the white man's arrival was a good thing, but that is not really relevant to this debate. At that time white men came to the coast for sea otter skins. They took them to China, sold them in Canton, and the result was the destruction of this animal on our coast.
We are fortunate that we have been able to restock the sea otter, which was done last year, and that this area is still wild and we can thus expect them to prosper. It is my hope that if we can prevent the careless exploitation, or even the most careful exploitation which involves a risk of destruction by oil leakage, we will preserve this area unspoiled for future generations who in turn will have some reason to give us thanks. Goodness knows, our generation has messed things up pretty badly in other areas.
I will turn now to the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra as well as the hon. member for Kootenay West regarding the responsibility of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. There is no doubt that outside the area which has been offered to the provincial government for their administration, he can completely ban offshore oil drilling. I might point out to hon. members opposite that it is precisely the efforts of members such as the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra, and other members of the Liberal Party who are working hard on the minister in this regard, which is most likely to result in success.

speechtext:
It may surprise the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) to know that I have visited the area. I wish to comment on something the previous speaker, the hon. member from Nova, said, namely, that the motion does not cover all parts of Canada and is not broad enough. In the area I come from, the government of Ontario-I need not remind hon. members of the political affiliation of that government-issues permits for oil drilling in the Great Lakes. Apparently it will continue issuing permits for oil drilling in Lake Erie.
Some of us are not too happy about this. One of the most amazing documents you could read is an IJC report concerning oil drilling operations in Lake Erie. About two years after I became a Member of Parliament I went to the township of Colchester bordering Lake Erie. There had been an oil leak, and all the beach fronting the lake had been fouled to such an extent that it could not be used by the people of the area.
I work with the Minister of Fisheries and Forestries (Mr. Davis) and I know how concerned he is about pollution. It is fair to say that all members of the House of Commons are concerned about pollution. Among other things the minister has said this, and I intend to put his remarks on record:
Think of an oil well in our shallow coastal waters just off the mouth of the Fraser River here in Vancouver. Think of an oil company striking an oil pool and then having its production get out of hand. Think of the damage to our local commercial and sports fisheries. Think of the damage to pleasure craft, beaches and recreation. Think of the downgrading of property values around the Gulf Islands and on Vancouver Island itself. Think even of the anguish of countless thousands of Canadians who might never see the oil scum but whose mental picture of the beauties of Georgia Strait would be shattered forever.

One of the earliest white settlers in my area was a French soldier whose diary before being translated into English was kept for many years in the museum at Fort Malden. In writing about the Detroit River he said there were so many fish there that he could walk across the river on the backs of fish of all species. He described the water-fowl of the area in glowing terms and said that the Detroit River and surrounding area was the most beautiful sight he had ever seen and was even more beautiful than the south coast of France.
We still have some water-fowl in the area, notwithstanding the pollution. Man has polluted the area, and man must clean it. We would not want the Georgia Strait to be polluted; no Member of Parliament would want that. I have been criticized in the past for not being more concerned about pollution. Pollution, it seems, is uppermost in the minds of Canadians no matter where they live. I can remember when I was reeve of my municipality trying to obtain a lagoon, a pollution control system for the region, only to be practically assassinated by innuendo. It was said the lagoon was not necessary.
That was ten years ago. Today, if you want to control pollution you are a hero; but it was not so ten years back, which is not so long ago. They did not think you were a saviour of mankind or of a country, as they do today, if you wanted to spend money on pollution control. Now they realize that pollution is terrible and is taking place in many parts of the country.
When we talk about oil drilling, whether it be on the west coast, the Arctic, the east coast or the Great Lakes, do hon. members realize how many square miles are involved? How big an area of our continental shelf are we talking about? In brief, our continental shelf covers a very large area of the east coast estimated to be approximately 430,000 square miles, extending seaward for 17 miles off Nova Scotia, 400 miles off Newfoundland and 75 miles near the eastern entrance to Hudson Strait. Off the west coast, the shelf is generally narrower but still extends seaward in places for 70 miles off the islet-fringed coast of British Columbia.
The area of the west coast shelf is estimated to be approximately 40,000 square miles. The submerged area in the Hudson Bay-Hud-son Strait region is estimated to be in the order of 400,000 square miles. The limits of

the shelf in the Arctic are not as well known as elsewhere, but the shelf has been estimated to be in the order of 500,000 square miles.
